Title: LSTM autoencoder based parallel architecture for deepfake audio detection with dynamic residual encoding and feature fusion
Text:
LSTM autoencoder based parallel 
architecture for deepfake audio 
detection with dynamic residual 
encoding and feature fusion
Priyanka Muruganandham, Govardhana Rajan Thangasamy, Sangeetha Jayaraman & 
Rekha Dharmarajan
With the rapid advancement of synthetic speech technologies, detecting deepfake audio has become 
essential for preventing impersonation and misinformation. This study aims to enhance detection 
performance by addressing limitations in existing models, such as temporal inconsistencies, weak 
contextual representation, and reconstruction loss. A novel framework, termed Long Short-Term 
Memory Auto-Encoder with Dynamic Residual Difference Encoding (LSTM-AE-DRDE), is proposed to 
overcome these challenges. The framework consists of two parallel modules: one leverages attention-
enhanced LSTM with contrastive learning to highlight critical temporal cues, while the other amplifies 
real-vs-fake separability by computing residual differences across transformed audio variants. 
By integrating diverse speech features-including MFCC, temporal, prosodic, wavelet packet, and 
glottal parameters the model captures both low- and high-level audio characteristics. Experimental 
evaluation was carried out on five benchmark datasets (CVoice Fake, FoR, Deepfake Voice Recognition, 
ODSS, and CMFD), where the proposed model achieved classification accuracies of 97%, 90%, 96%, 
97%, and 95%, respectively. Furthermore, when compared to eleven state-of-the-art methods, the 
proposed model demonstrates superior performance with an overall ROC-AUC of approximately 98%. 
In addition, a comprehensive feature-wise ablation study was conducted to assess the contribution of 
each feature set, confirming the robustness and reliability of the proposed framework.
Keywords  Deepfake audio detection, DRDE, LSTM-AE, Feature fusion model
Deepfake audio refers to artificially generated or manipulated voice recordings that closely mimic real human 
speech. These are produced using advanced AI techniques, including Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), 
Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), Diffusion Models (DMs), as well as sophisticated Text-to-Speech (TTS) and 
Speech-to-Speech (S2S) conversion models. Recent advancements in this field have led to the development of 
models such as Tacotron 2, which generates human-like speech from text, and WaveNet, a deep generative 
model capable of producing high-fidelity audio waveforms. Additionally, models like FastSpeech and VITS have 
improved the speed and quality of speech synthesis, enhancing the realism of generated audio. These technologies 
have significantly advanced synthetic speech generation, making it increasingly difficult to differentiate between 
real and fabricated voices.The widespread accessibility of deepfake audio has raised serious concerns regarding 
security, privacy, and misinformation. Studies suggest that human perception alone is often unreliable in 
detecting deepfake audio, emphasizing the urgent need for robust detection methodologies1–4 . Researchers 
are developing various countermeasures, including speech anomaly detection, AI-based forensic analysis, 
and authentication techniques, like digital watermarking, to verify the legitimacy of audio content2. Applying 
anti-spoofing techniques is also gaining traction, helping identify deepfake-generated voices more effectively4. 
Given the rapid evolution of deepfake technology, continuous advancements in detection and authentication 
mechanisms are essential to mitigate misuse and safeguard digital communications3.
The rapid advancement of deep learning techniques has led to the emergence of highly realistic deepfake 
audio, posing significant challenges in security, digital forensics, and media integrity5–7. AI-generated voices, 
produced by models such as WaveNet, Tacotron, and GAN-based architectures, can closely mimic human speech 
patterns, making them difficult to detect using traditional audio analysis methods8–10. In the literature, there are

For instance, the study by Mahum et al.14 proposed a model, DeepDet, which leverages Yet Another Mobile 
Network (YAMNet) combined with a bottleneck attention module (BAM) for detecting synthetically generated 
speeches. This study focuses on identifying TTS and VC based deepfake audio utilizing pre-trained audio 
embeddings from YAMNet and refining extraction through BAM to enhance the detection performance14. 
Similarly, the authors of Yang et al.15 employed a two-stream network which integrated Mel spectrogram-based 
features with raw waveform representations. This fusion enabled the model to capture fine grained spectral 
variations and temporal structures15. Another work Zhang et al.16 adopted the feature decomposition learning to 
separate the natural variations present in the human speech from artificial generation patterns. By isolating key 
spectral anomalies, this model achieved higher robustness across multiple synthesis methods16.
Authors of Zaman et al.17 leveraged self-attention mechanisms to capture the long-range dependencies in

proposed system implemented on ResNet, ECANet and SENet18. A distinct approach was proposed in Izotova 
et al.19 where speech signals were represented as graph structures allowing the model to capture the complex 
frequency-domain relationships. This approach is particularly effective in detecting subtle voice modifications 
applied by VC models. For real-time applications, proposed an efficient, low computation model that preserves

Twice Attention Networks (TA-networks) were introduced by Chen et al.25 which focused on detecting the 
artifacts in the synthetic speech samples. Their TA-Unet equipped with a five-layer U-Net with attention gates

spatial differences between left and right audio channels using a combination of channel specific, differential 
and invariant representations to detect deepfake artifacts. Collectively these studies highlight a transition from 
artifact-focused methods to frame-level and spatial-aware models, enhancing the accuracy and robustness27.
Recent advancements in deepfake detection have leveraged a combination of audio features such as MFCC, 
GTCC, ATP, and LFCC, integrated with deep learning architectures like ResNet50 and CNNs28,29. Frame-
level detection techniques have also emerged, enabling the localization of tampered audio segments with high 
precision30. In addition, spectrogram-based methods are employed to capture fine-grained frequency variations, 
while approaches like LDA and NNF enhance feature extraction efficiency. These methods have demonstrated 
high accuracy and low equal error rates (EERs) when evaluated on benchmark datasets such as ASVspoof 2019, 
ASVspoof 2021, VSDC, DECRO, and VIHL31–33. Current methods relying on real-audio training and histogram 
features lack robustness and generalizability against evolving and adversarial deepfake techniques34,35.
A diverse array of deepfake audio detection methods has emerged, spanning audio-specific, hybrid, and 
vision-inspired strategies. SC_Encoder and Whisper_Encoder architectures have been proposed for enhanced 
generalization36, while the DANet-ATP framework37 and classical classifiers such as LSTM and Random 
Forest focus on feature robustness and accuracy, though often limited by dataset dependency38. Waveform 
and spectrogram integration, along with reverberation modeling, have improved robustness but increased 
architectural complexity39,40. Some frameworks achieve impressively low equal error rates (EERs) using detailed 
pitch-based features, albeit at the cost of higher training overhead41. Multimodal systems combining CNNs, 
transformers, and feature fusion deliver strong performance but tend to rely heavily on visual features or demand 
significant computational resources42–44. Knowledge distillation frameworks have demonstrated promising 
improvements in detection accuracy but depend substantially on the quality and diversity of training data45.

Recent studies by Zhang et al. have introduced a range of visual deepfake detection techniques, including 
multi-scale attention mechanisms, dual-domain fusion modules, and attention-based CNN frameworks aimed at 
improving discrimination by capturing spatial and frequency features. Modules such as the Texture Suppression 
Module, Cross-Stream Interaction Module, and Cross-Stream Mix Block were shown to effectively reduce 
compression artifacts, which are also relevant to audio deepfakes. The ST-ILIF framework, in particular, focused 
on detecting temporal and spatial inconsistencies at the frame level, offering conceptual insights for potential 
adaptation to speech-based anomaly detection. Despite their effectiveness, all these methods are tailored for 
visual deepfake detection and require substantial modification for use in audio-specific tasks46–50.
To address these challenges, this study proposes a novel deepfake detection framework that begins by 
extracting multiple features, including Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCCs), Wavelet Packet 
Decompositon (WPD), Prosodic, Temporal features, and Glottal parameters. These features are then fused into 
a unified representation, which is fed into two parallel processing modules. The first module employs an LSTM 
autoencoder, integrated with contrastive learning and an attention mechanism. Contrastive learning optimizes 
feature representations in the latent space, enhancing the model’s ability to distinguish between real and fake 
audio. The attention mechanism further improves this process by focusing on the most discriminative parts 
of the input. The LSTM autoencoder reconstructs the audio, and the reconstruction error is used to measure 
the distinction between real and synthetic speech. The second parallel module, DRDE, processes the same 
fused features by applying multiple temporal transformations, such as time-reversing, pitch-shifting, and 
time-shifting. The differences between these transformed versions are computed and used to form a “dynamic 
difference signature,” which captures unique patterns distinguishing real from fake speech. The outputs of both 
modules are then combined to make the final prediction based on the majority reconstruction loss. By fusing the 
features at the outset and processing them in parallel, the model benefits from both the temporal dynamics and 
feature variations, improving the robustness and accuracy of deepfake audio detection.
Contributions of our research
This study makes the following key contributions:
•	 We design a comprehensive feature fusion strategy that combines MFCCs, WPD, Prosodic, Temporal, and 
Glottal features to form a unified and information-rich representation of speech signals.
•	 We propose a dual-path architecture consisting of an LSTM autoencoder with integrated contrastive learning 
and attention mechanisms, alongside a novel DRDE module that exploits temporal augmentations to capture 
fine-grained distinctions between real and fake audio.
•	 We implemented a combined decision-making scheme that aggregates outputs from both modules using 
majority reconstruction loss, which enhance detection accuracy by effectively leveraging both temporal dy­
namics and diverse feature variations.

subtle artifacts introduced by deepfake technologies. Our proposed framework integrates feature fusion, an 
LSTM Autoencoder, an attention mechanism for feature weighting and contrastive learning to enhance the 
deepfake audio detection.

This standardization allows the model to account for variations in the error distribution across different input 
audio samples and recording conditions. Since the reconstruction errors for genuine audio approximately follow 
a Gaussian-like distribution after normalization, the dynamic threshold is selected based on statistical confidence 
intervals derived from the current distribution rather than a fixed constant. This threshold adapts dynamically 
to each input audio, reflecting the natural variability in reconstruction error patterns. By using this adaptive 
thresholding mechanism, the model sets the threshold τ at a certain number of standard deviations (z-scores) 
above the mean error - typically within a range (e.g., between 1.5 and 3.0). This range balances the trade-off 
between sensitivity (detecting fake samples) and specificity (avoiding false alarms on real samples), and varies 
depending on the characteristics of the input data. Lower threshold values increase sensitivity but may produce 
more false positives, whereas higher values reduce false alarms but may miss subtle fake audio. Therefore, the 
threshold is not fixed but dynamically computed based on the statistical properties of the reconstruction errors, 
enabling robust and adaptive detection performance across varying audio inputs.
Experimental analysis
Dataset description
Fake or real (FoR) dataset
 FoR57 is a publicly available and widely used benchmark dataset for deepfake audio detection. It comprises 
over 195,000 utterances, including both authentic human speech and synthetically generated speech, and is 
specifically designed to facilitate the development and assessment of audio-based forgery detection systems. 
The FoR dataset includes four sub datasets, each tailored to simulate different experimental scenarios: for-
original, which contains raw audio recordings from diverse speech sources without modifications; for-norm, 
a standardized version of the original with balanced gender and class distribution along with consistent audio 
properties; for-2sec, featuring 2-second audio clips derived from for-norm to enable evaluation under limited-

It contains a total of 64 audio samples, including 8 real and 56 fake voice recordings. The fake samples are 
generated using Retrieval-based Voice Conversion (RVC) techniques, offering highly realistic synthetic speech. 
The dataset supports the development and evaluation of models capable of distinguishing between human and 
AI-generated voices.
Open dataset of synthetic speech (ODSS) dataset
 ODSS is a publicly available dataset developed to support research in synthetic speech detection59. It 
comprises 18,993 audio utterances generated using state-of-the-art speech synthesis methods, along with their 
corresponding natural (real) counterparts. The dataset includes 156 voices spanning three languages: English 
(en), German (de), and Spanish (es), with balanced gender representation across speakers. For our study, we 
utilize only the English subset. This subset contains a total of 48 folders, representing both real and fake speakers, 
and each folder contains 63 audio files. This organization allows systematic training, validation, and testing to 
evaluate within-dataset model performance. ODSS is released under the CC-BY-SA 4.0 license, promoting open 
access, reproducibility, and further development by the research community.
Copy-move forgery detection (CMFD) dataset
 CMFD is a publicly available dataset specifically collected for research in detecting audio forgeries created 
using copy-move techniques60. It contains audio samples in two languages: English and Chinese. Each subset 
includes 1800 real and 1000 fake audio samples, bringing the total to 3600 real and 2,000 fake samples across 
both languages. For our study, we utilized only the English subset, which comprises 1800 untampered (real) and 
1000 tampered (fake) audio files. For effective training, validation, and testing, the dataset was split accordingly 
to support within-dataset performance evaluation, as detailed in Table 1.
CVoice fake (CVF) dataset
 The CVoiceFake dataset is a multilingual deepfake audio collection that includes real (Bonafide) and fake speech 
samples in five languages: English, Chinese, German, French, and Italian61. The fake audios are generated using 
six different voice cloning models-Parallel WaveGAN, Multi-band MelGAN, Style MelGAN, Griffin-Lim and 
WORLD-each contributing to the diversity and realism of the synthetic speech. Although the dataset covers 
multiple languages and synthesis techniques, we have used only the English language samples for our study. For 
this, the total number of bonafide (real) audio samples used is 4315, and among the five generated fake folders, 
we utilized only one synthetic generation folder, which also contains 4315 fake audio samples. This dataset has 
been utilized specifically for testing the performance of our proposed deepfake audio detection model. Table 2 
summarizes the distribution of the dataset used for training, validation, and testing, providing an overview of 
the within-dataset performance evaluation.

Conclusion
This study proposes a novel framework for deepfake audio detection that emphasizes the effectiveness of 
fusing multiple feature sets-including MFCCs, Wavelet Packet Decomposition, prosodic, temporal, and glottal 
parameters-into a unified representation. This fusion enhances the model’s ability to capture both fine-grained 
and broad variations in speech signals, improving its ability to distinguish between real and synthetic audio. 
The unified features are processed in parallel by two modules: an LSTM autoencoder enhanced with attention 
and contrastive learning, and a Dynamic Residual Difference Encoding (DRDE) module that extracts residual 
patterns through temporal transformations. The fusion of both modules enables the detection of subtle and 
complex inconsistencies in synthetic audio. Experimental evaluation shows that the proposed model outperforms 
existing methods, achieving a robust ROC-AUC score of 98%.
As a future direction, we plan to extend this audio-based system by incorporating video modalities, such as 
facial movements and lip-sync consistency, to create a more comprehensive multimodal detection framework. 
This will enable deeper cross-modal validation and improve detection performance in complex real-world 
scenarios.
